question: What is the primary function of antigens found on the surface of red blood cells?

options.A: Producing clotting factors to stop active bleeding
options.B: Regulating the overall pH balance of plasma
options.C: Acting as molecular markers that the immune system recognizes
options.D: Transporting oxygen molecules directly to body tissues

explanation: Antigens sit on red blood cells like name tags, helping the body tell its own cells apart from foreign invaders. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h1)

question: What happens when antibodies in a patient's plasma encounter unfamiliar red blood cell antigens?

options.A: They convert the foreign antigens into safe body proteins
options.B: They absorb the extra antigens to nourish surrounding tissues
options.C: They dissolve the donor red blood cells into liquid plasma
options.D: They bind to the foreign cells and cause agglutination

explanation: Plasma antibodies attack unfamiliar antigens by latching onto them, which makes the red blood cells clump together. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which antibodies are naturally present in the plasma of a person with Type A blood?
explanation: Type A blood has A antigens on the cells, so the body develops anti-B antibodies to attack foreign B types. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h2)

question: A patient with Type AB blood needs an emergency red blood cell transfusion. Why are they called universal red cell recipients?

options.A: Their red blood cells contain no surface antigens
options.B: Their body rapidly destroys all incoming donor antibodies
options.C: Their immune system is completely inactive during stress
options.D: Their plasma lacks both anti-A and anti-B antibodies

explanation: Because Type AB plasma does not contain anti-A or anti-B antibodies, it will not attack incoming red blood cells from other ABO groups. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h2)

question: What determines whether a person is considered Rh-positive?

options.A: The presence of the D antigen on their red blood cells
options.B: The presence of anti-Rh antibodies floating in their plasma
options.C: The presence of both A and B antigens on their platelets
options.D: The total volume of hemoglobin circulating in their blood

explanation: The term Rh-positive simply means the red blood cells carry the D antigen on their outer surface. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h3)

question: Why is an Rh-negative mother at risk when carrying an Rh-positive baby for the second time?

options.A: Her plasma lacks enough iron to support two separate blood supplies
options.B: Her immune system has already formed antibodies against the Rh factor
options.C: Her baby will automatically inherit a mismatched ABO blood type
options.D: Her bone marrow stops producing red blood cells during late pregnancy

explanation: Exposure during the first pregnancy sensitizes the mother, prompting her body to build antibodies that can attack a later Rh-positive baby. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of mixing a patient's blood with anti-A serum in the laboratory?

options.A: To determine the total volume of plasma in the patient's body
options.B: To measure the exact amount of white blood cells in circulation
options.C: To check if A antigens are present on the red blood cells
options.D: To destroy any harmful bacteria hiding inside the blood sample

explanation: Clumping with anti-A serum proves that the patient's red blood cells carry the A antigen. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the most immediate danger when a patient receives an incompatible blood transfusion?

options.A: Rapid growth of abnormal white blood cells in the bone marrow
options.B: Complete permanent loss of natural immunity to infections
options.C: Sudden permanent paralysis of the skeletal muscles
options.D: Destruction of red blood cells leading to kidney damage

explanation: Incompatible transfusions cause red blood cells to burst, releasing free hemoglobin that clogs and damages the kidneys. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the main difference between routine blood typing and a cross-match?

options.A: Blood typing requires samples from both the donor and recipient families
options.B: Cross-matching tests for hidden incompatibilities beyond basic ABO and Rh types
options.C: Cross-matching measures the exact amount of oxygen in donor plasma
options.D: Blood typing is only performed after a transfusion has already started

explanation: Cross-matching is a direct laboratory test that checks for reactions against minor antigens that standard typing misses. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h5)

question: What does a major cross-match involve in the laboratory?

options.A: Mixing the donor's serum with the donor's own plasma
options.B: Checking the donor's white blood cell count under a microscope
options.C: Mixing the recipient's serum with the donor's red blood cells
options.D: Testing the recipient's urine for traces of breakdown proteins

explanation: The major cross-match checks if the patient's antibodies will attack the donor's red blood cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h5)

question: How many licensed nurses must verify patient identification and blood bag details at the bedside before starting a transfusion?
explanation: A mandatory two-nurse bedside check prevents dangerous clerical errors and mismatched transfusions. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h6)

question: A nurse is preparing to start a blood transfusion for an adult patient. Which intravenous solution should be used to prime the Y-tubing?
explanation: Normal saline (0.9% sodium chloride) is isotonic and compatible with red blood cells, preventing hemolysis that other solutions might cause. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the very first action a nurse must take if a patient shows signs of a blood transfusion reaction?

options.D: Slow down the infusion pump rate

explanation: Stopping the infusion cuts off any further entry of incompatible or reactive blood products into the patient's circulation. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h7)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of circulatory overload during a blood transfusion?

options.A: Shortness of breath and crackles in the lungs
options.B: Sudden widespread hives and severe skin itching
options.C: High fever accompanied by uncontrollable shivering
options.D: Sharp pain radiating into the lower back area

explanation: Circulatory overload occurs when fluid volume overwhelms the heart, leading to pulmonary congestion and breathing difficulty. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h7)
